lines.text: not believe on me" means that the world fails to recognize
Him who, sent by God, stands over against it, accuses it,
rejects its claim to be inherently powerful and self-sufficient,
unmasks its limitedness, its questionableness, and its lack of
sanctity. To refuse to believe on Jesus does not mean to
reject as incredible some curious doctrines about Him, but
to refuse to allow His validity as God's challenge to the
world, to close one's eyes to the intrinsic finiteness of earthly
things, to consider the world the final authority both in
what it claims and in what it offers, to shut oneself off from
the grace which flows from the holiness of God and is readily
available for this world as soon as it confesses that it needs
divine grace. This is sin.
Again, the Spirit convinces the world of the true meaning
of righteousness. The world too speaks of righteousness.
According to its own criteria it makes judgments, pro-
nounces one man to be right, another to be wrong, honours
one and defames another. And it makes especial use of the
principle that the course of history discloses judgment in that
it declares: in the successes and achievements of history, the
right is manifested. Right is what triumphs in the world.
In fact, the right and success are one and the same thing;
it supposes that, in the language of the gospel, righteousness
means the same thing as ascendancy and victory. But the
criteria of what may be called victory differ. The judgment
of the world presupposes that victory must be revealed in
what is visible, and failure in the visible sphere spells defeat
and destruction. But the Spirit teaches us thus: "Of
righteousness because I go to the Father and you will see
me no more." This is very remarkable: Jesus' failure in the
visible sphere, His death and His departure from the world
is His victory! He has overcome the world, and His death is
the very confirmation and seal of His work which was to
confront the world with God's challenge to it. Had he
belonged to the world, then the world, which loves its own
(John 15: 19) would gladly have welcomed Him.
